entries.meaning: To change something completely, usually for the better. ---
examples: A coat of paint can transform a room.
The company transformed itself in five years.
The old factory is being transformed into apartments.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (transform a room), intransitive (the neighborhood transformed)

entries.meaning: To make a small change to something in order to improve it. ---
examples: Let me tweak the color a little.
He tweaked the recipe and it came out better.
They are tweaking the app before the launch.

entries.meaning: To move or change from one state, system, or job to another. ---
examples: The company plans to transition to solar power.
She transitioned from teaching to software work.
We are transitioning to the new system in March.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (transition the team to new software), intransitive (he transitioned to a new career)
entries.contrast: Transition takes to or into: transition to remote work.

entries.meaning: To develop gradually into a different or more advanced form. ---
examples: Languages evolve whether we like it or not.
The project evolved into something much bigger.
Their style has evolved over the years.

entries.meaning: To change the form or structure of something significantly. ---
examples: New rules could reshape the whole industry.
The storm reshaped the coastline.
Technology is reshaping how we work.

entries.meaning: To make something more modern by adding new methods or equipment. ---
examples: The city wants to modernize its buses.
They modernized the kitchen last year.
The airport is being modernized in stages.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (modernize a kitchen), intransitive (the industry has modernized)
entries.contrast: American spelling is modernize; British writing often has modernise.

entries.meaning: To change and improve the form or appearance of something. ---
examples: They plan to revamp the website.
The menu was revamped over the summer.
We are revamping the training program.

entries.meaning: To change or repair something thoroughly, from top to bottom. ---
examples: The state may overhaul its tax code.
They overhauled the engine last winter.
The whole system is being overhauled.
entries.contrast: Verb: oh-vur-HAWL. The noun (a complete repair) is OH-vur-hawl.

entries.meaning: To organize something in a new way, especially a company or a debt. ---
examples: The bank offered to restructure the loan.
They restructured the department last fall.
The company is restructuring again.

entries.meaning: To arrange something in a new and usually better way. ---
examples: We should reorganize the files by year.
She reorganized the whole closet in one afternoon.
The team is being reorganized under new management.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (reorganize the files), intransitive (the company reorganized)

entries.meaning: To make something bigger in size. ---
examples: We can enlarge the photo for the frame.
The shop enlarged its selection of bikes.
The waiting room is being enlarged.

entries.meaning: To increase or improve something, often quickly. ---
examples: A discount might boost sales.
The coach's speech boosted everyone's confidence.
They are boosting production before the holidays.

entries.meaning: To become three times as much, or to make something three times as much. ---
examples: Our costs could triple next year.
The town tripled in size after the factory opened.
Orders have tripled since the review came out.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (triple the order), intransitive (costs tripled)

entries.meaning: To become stronger or more extreme, or to make something so. ---
examples: The storm is expected to intensify overnight.
The pain intensified after an hour.
They have intensified the search along the river.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (intensify the search), intransitive (the storm intensified)
entries.contrast: -y becomes -ie-: intensifies, intensified; intensifying keeps the y.

entries.meaning: To become deeper or stronger, or to make something so. ---
examples: Silence can deepen a misunderstanding.
The crisis deepened over the winter.
Their friendship has deepened since the trip.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (deepen the channel), intransitive (the crisis deepened)

entries.meaning: To increase the range of something, or to become wider in range. ---
examples: Travel can broaden your view of the world.
The course broadened my interests.
They are broadening the program to include teenagers.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (broaden the program), intransitive (his tastes broadened)

entries.meaning: To make a feeling or an effect stronger, or to become stronger. ---
examples: Music can heighten the tension in a scene.
The delay heightened everyone's worry.
Security has been heightened at the airport.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (heighten the tension), intransitive (tension heightened)

entries.meaning: To increase suddenly and strongly. ---
examples: Demand tends to surge before the holidays.
Applications surged after the ad ran.
Energy prices have been surging since May.

entries.meaning: To raise something to a higher level, position, or quality. ---
examples: Good design can elevate an ordinary room.
The award elevated her to a new level of fame.
Elevating your leg will help with the swelling.

entries.meaning: To become less in number or amount, or to make something less. ---
examples: Sales usually decrease in January.
The number of accidents decreased last year.
Rainfall has been decreasing for a decade.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (decrease the dose), intransitive (sales decreased)

entries.meaning: To become smaller or less important, or to make something seem so. ---
examples: Nothing can diminish what she did that night.
His influence diminished over the years.
The pain has been diminishing since Friday.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (diminish someone's role), intransitive (the noise diminished)

entries.meaning: To become less, or to make something less. ---
examples: A hot drink may lessen the pain.
The risk lessened after the second dose.
The medicine is lessening the swelling.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (lessen the pain), intransitive (the pain lessened)
entries.contrast: Lessen (make less) sounds exactly like lesson (a class).

entries.meaning: To become less wide, or to reduce something to fewer choices. ---
examples: The road narrows past the bridge.
We narrowed the list to three names.
The gap has been narrowing since spring.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (narrow the list), intransitive (the road narrows)

entries.meaning: To become gradually smaller or fewer until little is left. ---
examples: Supplies dwindle fast in a storm.
The crowd dwindled to about twenty people.
Our savings have been dwindling all year.

entries.meaning: To fall very fast and very far. ---
examples: Prices can plummet overnight.
The stock plummeted after the news.
Temperatures have been plummeting all week.
entries.contrast: The stress is on the first syllable, so the t does not double: plummeted, plummeting.

entries.meaning: To use up most of the supply of something. ---
examples: A long winter can deplete the whole supply.
The drought depleted the reservoir.
Their savings have been depleted by medical bills.

entries.meaning: To increase the quality, value, or attractiveness of something. ---
examples: A little salt will enhance the flavor.
The lighting enhanced the photos.
They are enhancing the security of the app.

entries.meaning: To make a process simpler and more efficient. ---
examples: We should streamline the hiring process.
They streamlined the menu down to ten dishes.
The office is streamlining its paperwork.

entries.meaning: To improve the quality or value of something by adding to it. ---
examples: Reading will enrich your vocabulary.
Compost enriched the soil.
The program has enriched the whole community.
entries.contrast: The third person adds -es after -ch: enriches.

entries.meaning: To fill something up again after it has been used. ---
examples: We need to replenish the supplies.
The rain replenished the reservoirs.
Shelves are being replenished every morning.

entries.meaning: To stop developing or improving. ---
examples: Wages can stagnate for years.
The project stagnated after the manager left.
The economy has been stagnating since 2022.

entries.meaning: To recover and rise again after a fall or a setback. ---
examples: Markets usually rebound after a shock.
Sales rebounded in the fall.
The team has rebounded from a terrible start.
entries.русский: восстанавливаться, идти вверх после падения; отскакивать
entries.contrast: Verb: rih-BOWND. The noun (on the rebound) is REE-bownd.

entries.meaning: To move forward or develop toward a better or later stage. ---
examples: The talks are finally starting to progress.
The illness progressed more slowly than expected.
Work is progressing well on the new wing.
entries.contrast: Verb: pruh-GRES. The noun (make progress) is PRAH-gres.

entries.meaning: To come out, or to become known, after being hidden or developing slowly. ---
examples: New details emerge every day.
He emerged from the meeting looking relieved.
A clear pattern has emerged from the data.
entries.contrast: Emerge from a place or a situation.

entries.meaning: To provide room for someone or something, or to change your plans to fit their needs. ---
examples: The hall can accommodate three hundred people.
They accommodated our request without complaint.
We are accommodating two extra guests this weekend.
entries.contrast: Two c's and two m's: accommodate.

entries.meaning: To make things follow one single standard or pattern. ---
examples: The state wants to standardize the tests.
They standardized the parts across all models.
Forms are being standardized department by department.

entries.meaning: To make something less extreme, or to become less extreme. ---
examples: Try to moderate your expectations.
He moderated his tone after the first question.
The heat has moderated since Sunday.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (moderate your tone), intransitive (the wind moderated)
entries.contrast: Verb: MAH-duh-rayt. The adjective (moderate prices) is MAH-duh-rit.

entries.meaning: To make something more difficult or more confusing than it was. ---
examples: Let's not complicate things.
The delay complicated our travel plans.
Rain is complicating the repairs.

entries.meaning: To change repeatedly up and down, or from one level to another. ---
examples: Gas prices fluctuate from week to week.
His weight fluctuated all winter.
The signal has been fluctuating since morning.

entries.meaning: To happen or to do something in turns, one after the other. ---
examples: We alternate weekends at my mother's house.
They alternated between English and Spanish.
Sunny days have been alternating with storms.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (alternate the shifts), intransitive (they alternated between two songs)
entries.contrast: Verb: AWL-tur-nayt. The adjective (an alternate route) is AWL-tur-nit.

entries.meaning: To vary between two limits. ---
examples: Tickets range from twenty to eighty dollars.
The answers ranged from angry to funny.
We saw cars ranging from tiny hatchbacks to old pickups.
entries.contrast: Range from one point to another.

entries.meaning: To stop happening, or to stop doing something — a formal word for stop. ---
examples: The noise did not cease until midnight.
The company ceased operations in March.
Fighting has ceased along the border.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive (cease operations), intransitive (the noise ceased)

entries.meaning: To begin again after a pause. ---
examples: We will resume right after lunch.
Play resumed once the rain stopped.
She has resumed her studies.
entries.contrast: Verb: rih-ZOOM. The noun résumé (a CV) is REZ-uh-may.

entries.meaning: To make something last longer. ---
examples: Nobody wants to prolong this meeting.
The treatment prolonged his life by years.
Arguing only prolongs the whole process.

entries.meaning: To keep something going at the same level over time.
examples: The soil cannot sustain that many crops.
They sustained the pace for two hours.
Growth has been sustained for six quarters.
